shape.name: Shape L - Pronunciation Noticing (Noticing-First)
shape.description: Noticing-first pronunciation lesson: learners are first made to hear the gap between their L1 transfer and the target feature (auditory discrimination), then the feature is isolated, explained, drilled, and used freely.
shape.pedagogical_justification: Pronunciation instruction that works is intelligibility-based (Levis, 2005; Munro & Derwing, 1995) and noticing-first (Schmidt, 1990). Learners must consciously notice a feature in input for it to become intake, and instruction is most effective when it primes that noticing (Schmidt & Frota, 1986). For Thai learners, word-final /t/ and /d/ are the critical case: Thai final stops are unreleased but phonologically present, so learners believe they are pronouncing the consonant when listeners hear nothing. Final-consonant deletion and missing clusters are the strongest intelligibility threats in Thai-accented English (Setter, 2005; Suntornsawet, 2022). The shape therefore follows the perception-before-production sequence established in final-consonant-deletion intervention: auditory discrimination precedes production. The trigger stage makes the gap audible by contrasting a model sentence against the L1-transfer version; the feature stage isolates the target (including the -ed /Id/ syllable, which Thai has no equivalent for) and links it to meaning (dropped -ed hides past tense); controlled production drills the release; freer use transfers it into spontaneous speech. Perceptual salience is designed in: model sentences place every target sound before a vowel or a pause, where native speakers audibly release the consonant. In-class data confirms the need: 112 students (27% of the cohort) carry examiner feedback flagging dropped or underarticulated final /t/, /d/, or -ed endings.
shape.main_aim_format: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to notice and produce [target feature] in the context of [topic].

example_lesson_plan.header:
Objective:
By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to notice and produce word-final /t/, /d/ and /Id/ endings (including -ed) in the context of talking about what they did last night.
Teacher:
Ed Rush
Date:
18 August, 2026
Duration:
46 minutes
CEFR Level:
B1
Lesson Shape:
L (Pronunciation Noticing)
Materials:
Slideshow, worksheet (Parts A-H), comparison audio, Part B and Part C tracks, Rome recording, quantum model audio
Assessment:
Discrimination accuracy (Parts A-C), production observation during drills and the game (Part F)
Systems:
Pronunciation

stages.stage_aim: To activate the topic and elicit the target feature in natural speech
procedure: Show the splash slide. Ask: What do you see? What might this lesson be about? Let students speculate.
Advance to the title slide. Confirm the theme: the sounds at the end of words.
Ask: What did you do last night? Elicit 3-4 answers. Write them on the board exactly as students say them, without comment.
Tell students the focus is the sounds at the END of words.

stages.stage_aim: To make the gap between L1 transfer and the target audible
procedure: Display the model sentence: I started my game at eight and played it all night.
Play the comparison track. Helen labels Thai English, then Standard English.
Ask: Can you hear the difference? What disappeared?
Students tap the table on every final /t/ or /d/ they hear in the Standard English version (Worksheet, Part A).
Feedback: the model sentence has five final sounds: started, eight, played, it, night.

stages.stage_aim: To perceive the target feature before producing it
procedure: Worksheet, Part B. Play the track: Helen announces each number, Benedict says each word twice.
Students write ✓ if both repetitions are correct, or ✗ if the final sound is dropped.
Check answers: pattern ✗ ✓ ✗ ✗ ✓.
Repeat any pairs students could not perceive. Note who still cannot hear the difference.

stages.stage_aim: To isolate the /t/, /d/, /Id/ endings and link them to meaning
procedure: Worksheet, Part C. Play the track: Russell reads each past-tense verb once. Students write ✓ if they hear the -ed ending, or ✗ if it is missing.
Check answers: wanted ✓, played ✗, stopped ✓, needed ✗, watched ✓, stayed ✓, started ✗, helped ✓.
Worksheet, Part D. Students clap the syllables. Reveal one count per click: wanted = 3, played = 1, stopped = 1, needed = 2.
Elicit the rule: after /t/ or /d/, -ed adds a syllable. Worksheet, Part E: circle the past tense - want is present, wanted is past.
Finger-tap drill on the model sentence: I started (1) my game at eight (2) and played (3) it (4) all night (5).
Backchain: night, all night, played it all night, I started my game at eight and played it all night.
Choral and individual drill. Whisper-release drill: night, played - the final consonant must be heard.
Correct errors immediately. -ed words keep their extra syllable.

stages.stage_aim: To transfer the feature into spontaneous speech
procedure: Worksheet, Part F. Show the game slide and start the 5-minute timer.
Pairs: A tells B two things they did last night. B holds up one finger for every final /t/ or /d/ heard - one point per sound.
Dropped final = do-over until B hears it. Swap after 2.5 minutes.
Content feedback first, then language feedback on the most frequent dropped finals.

stages.stage_aim: To consolidate noticing on authentic speech and set up recycling
procedure: Worksheet, Part G. Play Rome's book review. Students tick or cross the 23 numbered words. Reveal: only [5], [10], [22] and [23] were correct.
Worksheet, Part H. Play the quantum model. Pairs read the paragraph to each other and tick or cross.
Quick-fire exit: night, wanted, played. Say them with the ending.
Tell students the same finals return in the next lesson's warm-up.

materials: Audio: model-sentence comparison track (Helen labels Thai English and Standard English)
Audio: Part C past-tense verbs track
Audio: Rome's book review recording (Part G)
Audio: quantum theory model reading (Part H)
metadata.main_aim: By the end of the lesson, learners will be better able to notice and produce word-final /t/, /d/ and /Id/ endings (including -ed) in the context of talking about what they did last night.
metadata.subsidiary_aim: To link dropped -ed endings to lost past-tense meaning and transfer the feature into pair interaction.
answer_key: Part A - Can you hear it? The model sentence has five final sounds: started (/Id/), eight (/t/), played (/d/), it (/t/) and night (/t/).
Part B - Same or different? Pattern: night ✗, fight ✓, last ✗, wanted ✗, played ✓. The dropped endings were nigh(t), las(t) and wante(d).
Part C - Past tense or not? wanted ✓, played ✗, stopped ✓, needed ✗, watched ✓, stayed ✓, started ✗, helped ✓. Words 2, 4 and 7 lost the whole -ed syllable: play, need, start.
Part D - The -ed pattern. Syllables: wanted = 3, played = 1, stopped = 1, needed = 2. After /t/ or /d/, -ed adds a syllable.
Part E - Does the ending matter? The past-tense words are wanted and played. Night ends with a /t/ sound.
Part G - Rome's book review. Rome pronounced only [5], [10], [22] and [23] correctly. The other 20 endings were dropped.
